title: How SNAP Theft Happens — and What to Do if It Happens to You

sections.title: Conversation 1
sections.scene: A university financial aid adviser and a student discuss a stolen meal-card balance and how to prevent further loss.

script.en: Come in, Jason. You said on the phone that your meal-card balance disappeared overnight. That's the second case I've heard this week.

Exactly. I checked the app last night before bed and had about three hundred dollars left. This morning it showed zero, and there were purchases at a convenience store two miles off campus that I've never been to.

That pattern is consistent with what campus security has been reporting. Someone likely attached a small reading device to the card reader at the dining hall entrance. When you tapped your card, it copied your account information.
So the machine at the door was compromised? I thought those readers were supposed to be secure.

They are, in theory. But the older models rely on magnetic strips, and those can be copied in seconds. The university has been slow to upgrade because the newer chip-enabled readers cost more and require replacing hundreds of units across campus.
That's frustrating. So what do I do now? Is the money just gone?

You need to file a formal report with the card office today. Under the new policy, if the theft is verified within five business days, you can be reimbursed up to the full amount. But you must also freeze the card immediately through the mobile app.
I didn't know the app had a freeze function. I only use it to check my balance.

It does, and it's the single most effective step. You can also set up alerts for any transaction over twenty dollars. That way, if someone tries to use your card again, you'll know within minutes rather than hours.
I'll do that right away. But honestly, shouldn't the university be responsible for securing the readers in the first place? Why should students have to monitor every purchase?

I understand the frustration, and many students have raised the same point. The administration is reviewing the issue, but until the hardware is replaced, individual vigilance remains the most reliable safeguard. I'll email you the reimbursement form and a guide to the app's security settings.
Thanks. I appreciate the help, even if the system itself seems backwards.

script.en: Electronic benefit cards were introduced decades ago as a convenient replacement for paper food stamps. Today, they serve millions of households, yet the technology behind them has remained surprisingly outdated. Unlike modern credit cards, which use microchips and tap-to-pay features to protect transactions, most benefit cards still rely on magnetic strips that can be copied with inexpensive devices. This gap has created an opening for criminal organizations, and skimming devices, often installed on card readers at grocery stores, capture account data and personal identification numbers. The information is then used to drain benefits, sometimes within hours. In one recent year, nearly half a billion dollars was stolen from recipients, affecting close to a million households. Victims often face a confusing recovery process. While some states have begun to offer reimbursement, the rules vary widely, and many recipients are unaware of deadlines or needed paperwork. Advocates argue that the burden should not fall on people who have already been harmed. They point out that banks have largely solved similar problems for credit card users through chip technology and automatic fraud alerts. Why, then, has the upgrade been so slow? Officials cite the cost of replacing millions of cards and the complexity of coordinating across federal and state agencies. Some also note that benefit programs are designed to prioritize quick delivery of aid, not long-term security. As a result, recipients are often advised to lock their cards, change passwords often, and monitor accounts—measures that are difficult for elderly or disabled users. The debate in the end concerns responsibility, and if the government provides a payment system, should it also guarantee its security? For now, the answer remains unclear, and millions of vulnerable households continue to bear the risk.

sections.title: Stolen Benefits, Stalled Solutions
sections.passage:
When Kelly Joly tried to buy groceries for herself and her teenage son at a Kroger in Beaumont, Texas, this August, her electronic benefits transfer card was declined. She had received her monthly $530 in Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program benefits the day before, but her account now showed transactions at stores in Illinois, Minnesota and California. A representative at the Texas agency overseeing SNAP told her there was nothing they could do to replace the funds. Joly's experience is far from isolated: last year alone, more than $470 million was stolen from SNAP recipients by card scammers, affecting about 990,000 households.

Much of this crime is the work of low-level street operatives for transnational criminal organizations who install "skimming" devices on card readers at local grocery stores and bodegas. When a recipient swipes a card, these devices capture data from the magnetic strip on the back, as well as the personal identification number. That data is either picked up later or transmitted via Bluetooth to thieves waiting nearby. Skimming is largely preventable through microchips and tap-to-pay technology, which have greatly reduced fraud in credit and debit card transactions for over a decade. But efforts to install these chips in EBT cards have moved much more slowly.

In recent years, criminals have also used random number generators, phishing calls and spam texts to steal card information, and they will call state hotlines to try to check a recipient's SNAP balance and deposit date. In other instances, corner store owners themselves are in cahoots with scammers, ringing up fake grocery purchases in exchange for cash. And in at least one prominent case, a federal SNAP employee gave sensitive data to criminals for them to be able to steal benefits.

Unfortunately, due to the government's inaction, the burden of protecting benefits has largely been left to individual recipients. Phone apps such as ebtEdge or Propel allow users to track card balances, monitor transaction history for suspicious purchases and lock cards when they are not in use. These apps may also permit users to change PINs and block out-of-state or online transactions. But these are not always practical solutions. Remembering new PINs constantly, for example, is not easy, especially for older beneficiaries.

Cynthia Clark, a 63-year-old retired special education teacher in Jackson, Tennessee, said she has several health conditions that affect the dexterity of her hands, her vision and at times her speech. After her SNAP benefits were stolen in May, she was advised to lock her card every time she was not using it. But she said her disabilities make using a cellphone incredibly difficult. On more than one occasion, she has locked herself out of her SNAP account trying to access her benefits.

The debate ultimately concerns responsibility. If the government provides a payment system, should it also guarantee its security? For now, the answer remains unclear, and millions of vulnerable households continue to bear the risk.

long_sentences.en: As part of this reporting, we gathered detailed accounts from more than 50 people across 18 states who’ve had their benefits stolen in the past five years and reviewed dozens more messages, comments and social media posts from people who said they were targeted.

In recent years, criminals have also used random number generators, phishing calls and spam texts to steal people’s card information, and they will call state hotlines to try to check your SNAP balance and deposit date.
Phone apps, like ebtEdge or Propel , allow you to keep careful track of your card balance, monitor your transaction history for any suspicious purchases and lock your card when it isn’t in use.
